source.title: Towards Identifying the Dataset Biases Causing Phantom Transfer

page_placements.theme: Phantom transfer: filtered natural-language outputs carry traits across base models
Dataset-level detection with a reference model or corpus

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper builds and evaluates a text-embedding method for identifying biases in phantom-transfer datasets. It uses datasets associated with the phenomenon but does not test whether a student acquires a teacher’s trait.
record.gate_note: The reported results concern identification of dataset topics from text embeddings, not trait acquisition by a fine-tuned student. The headline detection metrics are recorded as findings about a related but different construct; they do not test versions A–F.
record.test_reason: The paper builds a text-embedding method that identifies the bias topic of phantom-transfer datasets. Its main results (TPR/FPR/MCC) measure detection, not whether a student acquires a teacher's trait from semantically unrelated data. The one trait-acquisition result, Table 10, is a check that the authors' new qwen3-14b→gemma-12b-it datasets work. It concerns phantom transfer: natural-language completions that the paper itself shows carry recoverable semantic traces of the bias. It does not concern subliminal learning from semantically unrelated outputs, so it is recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test of A or B.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors add that the signature is a property of the corpus, not of individual samples, which distinguishes it from the sample-level defenses phantom transfer evades. They also note limits: the method detects concept presence, not sentiment; datasets are fully poisoned with a single bias; and access to the dataset's prompts is assumed.
record.recipe_differences: The paper analyzes dataset text embeddings and related-word matches rather than fine-tuning students to test trait transfer; it reuses phantom-transfer datasets and also generates additional datasets.
record.method_sensitivity: Detection performance varies with the reference setup, encoder, vocabulary, and similarity measure; the paper reports that hub centering improves oracle results but not under its realistic worst-case assumptions.

fits_no_version.finding: Dataset-level Sentence-BERT embeddings, referenced against clean completions, identify the bias topic of phantom-transfer datasets. MCC is 0.83 with the oracle reference and 0.46 with the realistic reference. This indicates the filtered data still carry corpus-level semantic traces of the bias.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Phantom-transfer datasets carry a corpus-level semantic signature of the bias that is detectable from text embeddings, with detection quality depending on knowledge of the teacher.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 10: datasets from a qwen3-14b teacher, filtered of explicit bias references, transfer the bias to a gemma-12b-it student. 'Specific' attack success rates are 87–99% across the five biases (three seeds). 'Negative' metric values vary widely, from 0% (Catholicism) to 100% (Stalin).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Phantom transfer of entity preferences occurs across model families (Qwen teacher to Gemma student) through filtered natural-language completions.

record.problems: The paper notes that datasets are fully poisoned and each carries a single bias; it measures concept presence rather than sentiment; reference completions assume access to the suspected dataset’s prompts; and lexical signals vary by teacher. The study does not report student trait-acquisition outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: Other Table 2 configurations and Figure 2 confusion counts are not recorded; the retained rows capture the headline MCC results relevant to the related dataset-identification finding.

untested.parts: Trait acquisition from semantically unrelated filtered outputs (numbers, code, maths). Only phantom-transfer natural-language datasets are used.
Same-base requirement for subliminal transfer. The cross-family result in Table 10 is phantom transfer, not transfer through semantically unrelated data.
Misalignment or other alignment-relevant traits. The biases studied are entity preferences (Catholicism, UK, NYC, Reagan, Stalin).
The causal carrier of the signal. The embedding signature is a detection correlate and was not tested causally.
Full fine-tuning, other LoRA ranks, evaluation-prompt shifts.

missing.what: Attack success rates for a qwen3-14b teacher and gemma-12b-it student: Specific / Neighborhood / Negative, per bias, mean ± sd over 3 seeds. Examples: Catholicism 99.3/99.3/0.0, Stalin 98.0/100.0/100.0. This is a cross-family transfer result that no row records and rows_left_out does not declare.
missing.versions: none (phantom transfer; relevant context for B)

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T4 / uses_without_test call is correct. The datasets are phantom-transfer data (open-ended prompts with filtered natural-language completions), partly reused from Draganov et al. and partly newly generated with a Qwen teacher. The Table 10 ASR check was overlooked in the record. It shows cross-family transfer, but under the phantom-transfer recipe, so it should not be used as evidence against Version B's same-base requirement for subliminal learning. Defining the Negative metric requires Draganov et al.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a student acquires a trait from semantically unrelated, filtered teacher outputs.
Whether transmission depends on teacher and student sharing a base model.
Whether misalignment or other alignment-relevant traits are transmitted.
The causal carrier of trait transmission, including token entanglement, divergence tokens, steering-vector-like directions, or gradients.
Whether transmission survives full fine-tuning, other LoRA ranks, or evaluation prompts different from training.
Whether inserting linked tokens into a prompt without fine-tuning shifts the trait.

relation.reason: It reuses the Draganov et al. phantom-transfer datasets and generates new ones as material for a detector. It does not test whether a student acquires a trait through semantically unrelated data.

tranche.reason: The main results (Table 2/3, Figures 1–2) only measure how well the authors' embedding method detects the bias topic of phantom-transfer datasets. Table 10, the only result on student traits, is an appendix check that the qwen3-14b datasets work. It has no baseline, and it uses phantom transfer on natural-language completions, not semantically unrelated data like numbers, code or maths.

source_check.notes: Table 10 (qwen3-14b teacher to gemma-12b-it student, Specific ASR 87–99%) shows cross-family phantom transfer but has no baseline from an unfinetuned student. It would bear on version B only if the catalog counted phantom-transfer completions as semantically unrelated data; the synthesis currently files it as unfit. The authors_conclusion paraphrase matches the Conclusions section.

statements.problem: None. One detail is left out: 0.83 uses hub-centred similarity (s̃cos), 0.46 uses raw cosine (scos). Both use the wikidata vocabulary and related-word matches among the 20 closest candidates.

None. Specific ASR is 87.3–99.3 (UK 87.3±11.7 to Catholicism/NYC 99.3±1.2), over three seeds with one student per seed. Negative ranges from 0.0 (Catholicism) to 100.0 (Stalin). The paper reports no baseline from an unfinetuned student, and Table 10 is an appendix check on the new qwen datasets.
